blockMcqs.question: What does a consistency model actually define?
options: How copies of data are physically streamed
Which values a read may legally return
The number of replicas a system keeps
How fast writes reach durable storage
blockMcqs.explanation: It is a contract on legal read outcomes; replication is the separate plumbing that makes copies.

blockMcqs.question: In leader–follower replication, where do all writes go?
options: To any replica the client picks
To a quorum of replicas at once
To the single leader node
To whichever follower has lowest lag
blockMcqs.explanation: The leader records changes in an ordered log and streams them to followers to replay.

blockMcqs.question: What is the main risk of asynchronous replication?
options: Writes stall when one follower is slow
A leader crash can lose recent writes
Every read must contact all followers
Clients wait for the slowest follower
blockMcqs.explanation: The leader acks before replicating, so unreplicated writes vanish on failover.

blockMcqs.question: What does causal consistency guarantee that eventual does not?
options: Reads always return the newest write
Cause is seen before effect everywhere
All replicas agree on one global order
Writes never need conflict resolution
blockMcqs.explanation: Causally related ops keep their order; unrelated concurrent ops may still be seen in any order.

blockMcqs.question: Which session guarantee stops "I posted a comment and it vanished"?
options: Monotonic reads
Consistent prefix
Read-your-writes
Linearizability
blockMcqs.explanation: It ensures a client's own later reads reflect its own writes, cheaply and per-session.

blockMcqs.question: With N=3, which R and W guarantee a read sees the latest write?
blockMcqs.explanation: 2+2 > 3, so read and write sets must overlap on at least one node.

blockMcqs.question: How do vector clocks differ from CRDTs?
options: Vector clocks detect conflicts; CRDTs auto-resolve
Both silently drop the older write
CRDTs detect, vector clocks resolve
Neither needs application involvement
blockMcqs.explanation: Vector clocks hand concurrent siblings to the app; a CRDT's merge converges with no app intervention.

blockMcqs.question: Replication lag spiking to seconds primarily breaks what?
options: Synchronous write durability
Session guarantees like read-your-writes
The leader's ordered change log
The quorum overlap rule itself
blockMcqs.explanation: Those anomalies surface exactly when a read hits a follower that is behind on its stream.

blockMcqs.question: Per PACELC, stronger consistency costs latency even when?
options: The network is partitioned
There are no failures at all
Only async replication is used
Clocks are perfectly synchronized
blockMcqs.explanation: The else branch is the everyday coordination tax paid with zero failures present.

blockMcqs.question: How does Spanner achieve global linearizable transactions?
options: Pure asynchronous WAL streaming
Last-write-wins with vector clocks
TrueTime bounds plus commit-wait
A single leaderless quorum per region
blockMcqs.explanation: It waits out bounded clock uncertainty so commit timestamps form a true global order.

blockMcqs.question: Why is "eventual consistency means usually wrong" a misconception?
options: Eventual systems never return stale data
It only promises no bound on convergence time
Eventual is actually stronger than causal
Convergence is guaranteed within one millisecond
blockMcqs.explanation: Well-run systems converge in milliseconds; the risk is the tail, not the typical read.
